implementation_notes: On the JVM Kotlin uses java.lang.ThreadLocal exactly as Java does, but the usual Kotlin failure mode is suspension: a coroutine can resume on another thread, so a thread-local value is only stable if it is part of the coroutine context. kotlinx.coroutines bridges the two with ThreadLocal.asContextElement(value), which installs the value on resume and restores the previous one on suspension; for libraries that require real thread-local state (logging MDC, transactions) the underlying ThreadContextElement interface is the general mechanism. The classic key/collection structure is replaced by the ThreadLocal object plus the coroutine context element. Keep the plain ThreadLocal form for blocking thread-per-request code and for JVM APIs shared with Java.
pitfalls: asContextElement does not track mutations: a set() performed inside the coroutine is not propagated to the element and is lost at the next suspension - change the value with withContext instead.
Reading the ThreadLocal from a coroutine that does not carry the element yields an undefined value (the docs warn it may return either the old or the new value); use ensurePresent to fail fast.

A ThreadContextElement implementation must restore state correctly under interleaving suspensions and must not throw from updateThreadContext/restoreThreadContext - an exception leaves the coroutine context undefined.

variants.name: Coroutine context element (no ThreadLocal at all)
variants.idiom_name: custom CoroutineContext element + an accessor reading coroutineContext
variants.implementation_notes: When the state belongs to the coroutine rather than to the thread, no thread-local is needed: an immutable element in the CoroutineContext carries the value, an accessor reads it from coroutineContext, and structured concurrency propagates it to children automatically - the shape kotlinx.coroutines uses for CoroutineName and CoroutineExceptionHandler. Nothing is installed into the thread, so nothing can leak between coroutines that share a dispatcher thread. Use ThreadContextElement instead when a third-party API insists on thread-local state (that is what asContextElement builds on); use this variant for application-level request, tenant or trace context.
pitfalls: A mutable element breaks the contract: contexts are copied, compared and cached, so a fresh element per value must be created instead of mutating the one in place.
Accessing coroutineContext outside a suspend function (or in a launch whose context lacks the element) returns null - a typed accessor with an explicit failure is safer than a nullable default.
Work that escapes structured concurrency (GlobalScope, thread pools, callbacks) does not inherit the element and must receive the value explicitly.
